sections.title: Why Lakebase
sections.summary: Application teams struggle to choose, provision, scale and govern operational databases, especially across dev, test and production. Lakebase answers with serverless Postgres that separates compute from storage and lives inside the Data Intelligence Platform.
takeaways: Apps have become stateless, serverless and intelligent; databases have not kept pace
Separating compute from storage is what enables branching, scale to zero and fast recovery
Lower total cost comes from one governed platform, elastic compute and a better developer workflow

slides.title: What Lakebase is not for
slides.text:
What should you NOT do with Lakebase?
●
●
●
●
●
Large scale migrations. For customers considering PostgreSQL migration → use Lakegate
to assess readiness before committing (16 automated checks, readiness score, phased
migration playbook)
Migration from non-postgres databases (Especially true for GraphQL and NoSQL DBs!)
Run workloads which require more than:
○ 4000 concurrent connections
○ 16TB of Storage
Run OLAP workloads in an OLTP database, expecting improved performances (it won’t)
Splitting a large dataset into multiple branches or projects to workaround those
restrictions is strongly discouraged
slides.note: The current Autoscaling limit is 8 TB of logical data per branch, which differs from the 16TB shown on this slide. Confirm the current limit in the Lakebase documentation.

slides.title: Postgres extensions
slides.text:
Postgres Extensions
● We support an ever growing list of extensions, which are documented on our
website
● The list of available extensions can also be retrieved from Postgres directly
using SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions ORDER BY name;
● Installing an extension is as easy as CREATE EXTENSION <extension_name>;
● Amongst the popular extensions: pg_stat_statements (query metrics),
pgcrypto, pg_prewarm (cache prewarming), neon, postgis (geospatial),
pg_graphql (GraphQL support), pg_vector
OBS: We cannot support extensions that directly manipulate Postgres storage as this
would be incompatible with our storage infrastructure
slides.note: The supported extension list grows over time. Run SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions for the current list.

sections.title: Autoscaling deep dive
sections.summary: A look under the hood: stateless computes in front of multi-tenant storage made of safekeepers, pageservers and object storage, spread across availability zones for resilience.
takeaways: Writes are persisted to three safekeepers before they are acknowledged
Pages are served from pageservers and reconstructed from object storage when needed
Three availability zones and a standby pageserver give built-in redundancy

slides.title: Why autoscaling
slides.text:
Why Autoscaling?
Limitations of Traditional Monolithic PostgreSQL
●
Single point of failure results in downtime or data loss
○ Machine or datacenter failure
○ Disk failure
●
Scaling and Performance Limits
○ Inefficient resource utilization across storage/compute
○ Inefficient resource utilization across time (peak times)
●
Recovery and Resiliency
○ Slow restores from backups (dependent on storage size)
○ HA/DR complex to set up and maintain
●
High operational overhead
○ Capacity planning, backups, replication, failover, manual recovery, etc.

Reads: Compute reads from Pageserver. If the

Each Postgres instance uses 3 safekeepers located in different AZs. If one Safekeeper or AZ fails, the
system can still reach consensus. Built-in redundancy. Immediate recovery.
Each Postgres instance is hosted on two pageservers: one active node and one secondary failover
node, both nodes being located in different AZs. If a Pageserver fails, reads are automatically routed to
the secondary failover node. Recovery in a few seconds.
Object storage has built-in multi-AZ redundancy. Immediate recovery.
